transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

**Report PR-AUC as your headline number, and give ROC-AUC as a secondary one.**

**Why PR-AUC**
- With 3% positives, ROC-AUC can look good even when the model is poor for the retention team. Its false-positive rate divides by the huge pool of non-churners. A model can raise many false alarms and still post a high ROC-AUC. - PR-AUC tracks what your manager cares about: of the customers we flag, how many really churn (precision), and how many of the churners we catch (recall). - The baseline is clear. **Caveats**
- PR-AUC depends on the churn rate. Don't compare it across segments or periods with different rates unless you also show the baseline. - ROC-AUC is still useful as a measure of ranking quality that doesn't depend on the churn rate. Keep it as a supporting number. **What to add for a manager**
A single AUC rarely drives a decision. Add one line at the operating point your team can act on. For example: "If we contact the top N% by risk, we catch X% of churners, and Y% of those contacted would have churned." Pick N from the retention team's capacity. Compute all of these on a holdout set the model never saw, ideally split by time.

Thanks, I've looked at your table. It has 1,200 customers, with their plan, city, segment, how long they've been with you, monthly spend, recent support tickets, and a column called churned_next_month. What are you hoping to find out about your customers, and what would you do differently once you know it? For example, you might want to keep more of them from leaving, or understand who your best customers are.

i want to see the groups of customers, like which ones are different from each other. then i can treat each group different instead of all the same. the ones that leave too, i guess i want to know who they are.

So you want to see which kinds of customers you have and how they differ, so you can treat each group in its own way, and you'd also like to know who the customers that leave are. Your table already has a column called segment. Are those the groups you use today, or do you want to find new groups from how customers actually behave (spend, tenure, support tickets)?

hmm, i'm not sure how the segment column got made, someone set it up a while back. i'd rather see what actually makes them different, like how much they pay and how long they stay. whatever shows the real groups is fine.

Understood. I'll look for groups in how customers actually behave, mainly what they pay and how long they stay, and leave the old segment column aside. Then I'll show you how many in each group leave, so you can see who those customers are. One thing before I set it up: who will use these groups, just you, or a team (sales, marketing, support) who will need to read the results and act on them?
Just me, for now. I'm the one who will look at it and decide what to do.
